Force and Free-Body Diagrams: A force is a push or pull measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg m/s^2). Forces are vectors. A free-body diagram shows one object and only the forces acting on it, such as weight, normal force, tension and friction. The net force is the vector sum of all forces. Perpendicular forces combine with the Pythagorean theorem, and a force at angle theta has components F cos(theta) and F sin(theta). Contact forces need touching, while field forces such as gravity act at a distance.
Newton's First Law and Inertia: Newton's first law says an object keeps its state of rest or constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it. Inertia is the tendency to resist changes in motion, and mass measures it. When the net force is zero the object is in equilibrium, so it is at rest or moves at constant velocity with zero acceleration. A hanging object at rest has tension equal to weight, mg. A force is needed to change motion, not to maintain it.
Newton's Second Law: Newton's second law states that acceleration equals net force divided by mass: a = F_net / m, or F_net = ma. The acceleration points along the net force. One newton is one kilogram meter per second squared. Doubling the net force doubles the acceleration, and doubling the mass halves it. To solve problems, draw a free-body diagram, choose a positive direction, add forces with signs, and apply the law. Use the net force, not just the applied force.
Newton's Third Law and Weight: Newton's third law says that when A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different objects, so the forces never cancel each other. Equal forces can still give different accelerations because a = F / m. Mass is the amount of matter in kilograms, while weight is the gravitational force W = mg in newtons. On Earth g is 9.8 m/s^2. In an accelerating elevator the scale reads N = m(g + a) going up.
Friction and Inclined Planes: Friction opposes sliding between surfaces. Static friction rises to a maximum of mu_s N, and kinetic friction while sliding is mu_k N, where N is the normal force. On an incline of angle theta the weight splits into mg sin(theta) along the slope and mg cos(theta) perpendicular to it, so N = mg cos(theta). A frictionless slope gives a = g sin(theta). With friction, a = g sin(theta) - mu_k g cos(theta). At constant speed mu_k = tan(theta).
